questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding Breadth First Search (BFS) and Depth First Search (DFS) on an undirected simple graph [latex]G [/latex] is/are TRUE?

options.A: A DFS tree of [latex]G [/latex] is a Shortest Path tree of [latex]G [/latex].
options.B: Every non-tree edge of [latex]G [/latex] with respect to a DFS tree is a forward/back edge.
options.C: If [latex](u, v) [/latex] is a non-tree edge of [latex]G [/latex] with respect to a BFS tree, then the distances from the source vertex [latex]s [/latex] to [latex]u [/latex] and [latex]v [/latex] in the BFS tree are within [latex]\pm 1 [/latex] of each other.
options.D: Both BFS and DFS can be used to find the connected components of [latex]G [/latex].

questions.explanation:
Checking each BFS/DFS claim on an undirected simple graph:

- "A DFS tree is a shortest path tree": false — DFS explores as deep as possible along one branch first and gives no shortest-path guarantee at all; only BFS guarantees that.
- "Every non-tree edge w.r.t. a DFS tree is a forward/back edge": true — in an undirected graph, DFS can never produce a cross edge; every non-tree edge necessarily connects an ancestor-descendant pair (classified as a back edge, viewable from either endpoint as forward/back).
- "Non-tree BFS edge (u,v): distances differ by at most 1": true — this is a standard BFS property, since BFS explores level-by-level and any edge can only connect vertices in the same level or adjacent levels.
- "Both BFS and DFS can find connected components": true — running either traversal repeatedly from every yet-unvisited vertex correctly partitions the graph into its connected components.

Answer: The 2nd, 3rd, and 4th statements are all true.

questions.question: Let [latex]G[/latex] be any undirected graph with positive edge weights, and [latex]T[/latex] be a minimum spanning tree of [latex]G[/latex]. For any two vertices, [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex], let [latex]d_1(u, v)[/latex] and [latex]d_2(u, v)[/latex] be the shortest distances between [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex] and [latex]T[/latex], respectively. Which ONE of the options is CORRECT for all possible [latex]G[/latex], [latex]T[/latex], [latex]u[/latex], and [latex]v[/latex]?
questions.explanation:
[latex]T[/latex] is a subgraph of [latex]G[/latex] using only a subset of [latex]G[/latex]'s edges, so any path that exists inside [latex]T[/latex] between [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex] is also a valid path in [latex]G[/latex] (with the exact same total weight). This means the shortest path in [latex]G[/latex] can never be longer than the shortest path in [latex]T[/latex] — [latex]G[/latex] has strictly more routing options available (all of [latex]T[/latex]'s edges, plus possibly more), so it can only match or beat [latex]T[/latex]'s best distance.

So [latex]d_1(u,v)\le d_2(u,v)[/latex] always holds (equality is common but not guaranteed — a shortcut through a non-tree edge in [latex]G[/latex] can make [latex]d_1[/latex] strictly smaller).

Answer: [latex]d_1(u,v)\le d_2(u,v)[/latex]

[latex]10^{k}[/latex] records. Package A requires 0.0001[latex]n^{2}[/latex] time units and package B requires

Consider the weighted undirected graph with 4 vertices,where the weigh to edge {i, j} is given by the entry Wij in the matrix W.
[latex]W=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2&8 & 5\\ 2& 0& 5 &8 \\ 8 & 5 & 0& x\\ 5&8 & x&0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
The largest possible integer value of x, for which at least one shortest path between some pair of vertices will contain the edge with weight x is ____.

questions.question:
Let G be a simple undirected graph. Let TD be a depth first search tree of G. Let TB be a breadth first search tree of G. Consider the following statements.

(I) No edge of G is a cross edge with respect to TD. (A cross edge in G is between two nodes neither of which is an ancestor of the other in TD.)
(II) For every edge (u,v) of G, if u is at depth i and v is at depth j in TB, then |i-j|=1.

Which of the statements above must necessarily be true?
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- (I): in DFS of an undirected graph, every non-tree edge joins a vertex to its ancestor (back edge); cross edges cannot occur True
- (II): in BFS, an edge can join two vertices at the same depth (e.g. a triangle), so |i [latex]-[/latex] j| can be 0 False

Answer: I only

questions.question: The number of distinct minimum-weight spanning trees of the following graph is _______
questions.explanation:
Use Kruskal's idea.

- All four weight-1 edges (a-b, a-f, c-d, d-e) form no cycle, so every MST contains them. Components: {a, b, f}, {c, d, e}, {g}.
- Now g must be joined to both components using weight-2 edges:
[latex]\quad[/latex]g to {a, b, f}: g-a, g-b, g-f [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3 choices
[latex]\quad[/latex]g to {c, d, e}: g-c, g-d, g-e [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3 choices
- Weight-3 edges are never needed.

Number of MSTs [latex]=3\times3=9[/latex] (each of weight 8).

Answer: 9

The values of l(i,j) cannot be computed in either row major order or column

questions.question:
Consider a complete graph [latex]K_{n}[/latex] with [latex]n[/latex] vertices ( [latex]n>4[/latex] ). Note that multiple spanning trees can be constructed over [latex]K_{n}[/latex]. Each of these spanning trees is represented as a set of edges. The Jaccard coefficient between any two sets is defined as the ratio of the size of the intersection of the two sets to the size of the union of the two sets.

Which one of the following options gives the lowest possible value for the Jaccard coefficient between any two spanning trees of [latex]K_{n}[/latex] ?
questions.explanation:
The Jaccard coefficient between two spanning-tree edge sets is [latex]\dfrac{|E_1\cap E_2|}{|E_1\cup E_2|}[/latex], which reaches its lowest possible value [latex]0[/latex] precisely when the two spanning trees share no edges at all (completely edge-disjoint spanning trees).

In [latex]K_n[/latex] for [latex]n>4[/latex], there are more than enough edges ([latex]\binom{n}{2}[/latex] total, versus only [latex]n-1[/latex] needed per spanning tree) to always construct two entirely edge-disjoint spanning trees (this is guaranteed by well-known results on edge-disjoint spanning trees in dense graphs, e.g. via Nash-Williams/Tutte-style constructions). When the intersection is empty, the Jaccard coefficient is exactly [latex]0[/latex], which is also the theoretical minimum possible value for any Jaccard coefficient.

Answer: 0

questions.question:
An undirected graph G(V, E) contains n (n[latex]>[/latex]2) nodes named v1 , v2 ,...,vn. Two nodes vi , vj are connected if and only if 0[latex]\lt [/latex]|i-j|[latex]\leq[/latex]2. Each edge (vi,vj ) is assigned a weight i+j. A sample graph with n=4 is shown below.

What will be the cost of the minimum spanning tree (MST) of such a graph with n nodes?
questions.explanation:
Edge [latex](v_i,v_{i+1})[/latex] costs 2i + 1 and [latex](v_i,v_{i+2})[/latex] costs 2i + 2.

MST: [latex]v_1v_2[/latex] (3), [latex]v_1v_3[/latex] (4), and for each [latex]j\ge4[/latex] the cheaper edge [latex]v_{j-2}v_j[/latex] (2j [latex]-[/latex] 2).

[latex]3+4+\sum_{j=4}^{n}(2j-2)=7+(n^2-n-6)=n^2-n+1[/latex]

Answer: [latex]n^2-n+1[/latex]

questions.question:
Let [latex]G=(V,E)[/latex] be an undirected unweighted connected graph. The diameter of [latex]G[/latex] is defined as:
[latex]diam(G)=\displaystyle \max_{u,v \in V} \{ \text{the length of shortest path between }u \text{ and }v \}[/latex]

Let [latex]M[/latex] be the adjacency matrix of [latex]G[/latex].
Define graph [latex]G_2[/latex] on the same set of vertices with adjacency matrix [latex]N[/latex], where

[latex]N_{ij}=\left\{\begin{array} {lcl} 1 &\text{if}\; M_{ij}>0 \text{ or } P_{ij}>0, \text{ where }P=M^2\\0 &\text{otherwise} \end{array}\right.[/latex]

Which one of the following statements is true?
questions.explanation:
[latex]P=M^2[/latex] has [latex]P_{ij} \gt 0[/latex] exactly when there is a path of length 2. So in [latex]G_2[/latex], u and v are adjacent whenever their distance in G is 1 or 2.

A shortest path of length d in G can be covered with [latex]\lceil d/2\rceil[/latex] such jumps, so [latex]diam(G_2)=\lceil diam(G)/2\rceil[/latex].

Answer: [latex]diam(G_2)\le\lceil diam(G)/2\rceil[/latex]
